summary: Specifies the DetNet data plane for connecting Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN) networks across a DetNet MPLS network, so timing-sensitive traffic can cross a wider MPLS network.

eli5.summary: Two islands of exact-timing networks can be linked across a bigger network while still keeping their delivery promises.

questions: how to connect tsn networks over mpls
what is detnet tsn over mpls
how does tsn work over detnet
what is the detnet service proxy
subtitle: How Time-Sensitive Networking streams can be carried across a DetNet MPLS network.

tldr.problem: Separate IEEE 802.1 Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN) networks, built for bounded latency and no congestion loss, sometimes need to be joined across a wider network without losing those properties.
tldr.mechanism: Edge nodes treat each TSN Stream as an application flow of a DetNet MPLS flow, using the DetNet MPLS data plane of RFC 8964, with a service proxy that maps streams to DetNet flows.
tldr.outcome: The whole DetNet domain acts like one TSN relay node, and the MPLS headers are stripped at egress so the stream continues as a normal TSN stream.

today: RFC 9024 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2021, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It depends on the DetNet MPLS data plane of RFC 8964.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
The Time-Sensitive Networking Task Group in the IEEE 802.1 Working Group deals with deterministic services through IEEE 802 networks. Deterministic Networking (DetNet), defined by the IETF, is a service that a Layer 3 network can offer to DetNet flows. General background is in RFC 8655.

This document specifies using a DetNet MPLS network to interconnect TSN nodes or network segments. The DetNet MPLS data plane itself is defined in RFC 8964, and the reader is assumed to know the terminology of that and the DetNet architecture documents.
sections.eli5: Some networks promise exact timing. This RFC explains how to link such networks across a bigger network and keep the promise.

sections.title: The Scenario
sections.content:
DetNet edge nodes sit at the boundary of a DetNet domain. They map non-DetNet-aware Layer 2 traffic onto DetNet services and impose and remove the DetNet encapsulation. They are functionally similar to pseudowire terminating provider edge (T-PE) nodes that use MPLS-TE label switched paths, while transit nodes are label switching routers.

Edge nodes provide a service proxy that associates DetNet flows with native flows, so TSN Streams are treated as application flows by DetNet. The whole DetNet domain behaves as a TSN relay node for those streams, and the service proxy acts as a port of that relay node.

Packet replication and elimination points can sit in edge nodes and in relay nodes, conceptually parallel to L2VPN services.
sections.eli5: The edge of the tunnel is a doorway. It accepts TSN traffic, wraps it for the trip, and unwraps it at the other door.

sections.title: The Encapsulation
sections.content:
The DetNet MPLS data plane of RFC 8964 has two sub-layers. The service sub-layer follows pseudowire encapsulations and uses an S-Label and a DetNet control word (d-CW). The forwarding sub-layer follows MPLS Traffic Engineering and gives resource allocation and explicit routes through one or more F-Labels. Transit nodes only do forwarding sub-layer work, with no service sub-layer processing.

This document's approach is to treat a TSN Stream as an application flow from the DetNet MPLS point of view. A single DetNet MPLS flow can aggregate multiple TSN Streams.

Network fragmentation for DetNet is not supported and MUST be avoided, because it is inconsistent with the packet delivery times DetNet needs. When IP is the sub-network, IPv6 fragmentation MUST NOT be used and IPv4 packets MUST be sent with the DF bit set. The operator MUST ensure the DetNet encapsulation overhead plus the maximum TSN App-flow frame size does not exceed the DetNet network's MTU.
sections.eli5: The TSN message is put in an envelope with routing labels. The envelope must never be cut into pieces, because that would break the exact timing.

sections.title: Edge Node Procedures
sections.content:
Edge node behavior is split into three parts. The TSN part must comply with the relevant IEEE 802.1 standards. When a packet arrives from a customer edge, the node checks through Stream identification whether it belongs to a configured TSN Stream. If no stream matches and no other service is configured for the circuit, the packet MUST be dropped. If a stream matches, the stream-specific functions run, such as ingress policing or frame replication and elimination. With no stream-specific forwarding configuration, the PE MUST flood to other local customer edges and the proxy, or drop the packet if administrative policy does not allow flooding.

The service proxy maps between application flows and DetNet flows. It MUST check its mapping table for the packet's app-flow and, if found, associate the internal DetNet flow ID and forward it, otherwise it MUST drop the packet. Many-to-one mapping, aggregating multiple TSN Streams into one DetNet flow, SHALL be supported. Interworking between DetNet packet replication and TSN frame replication is out of scope and left for further study.

The service and forwarding sub-layer part follows RFC 8964, which supports 16-bit and 28-bit sequence numbers. Replication and elimination recovery is available only inside the DetNet domain, because the DetNet flow ID and sequence number are not valid outside it.
sections.eli5: The door checks each message is on the guest list, wraps the ones that are, and throws away the ones that are not.

sections.title: Management and Control Considerations
sections.content:
Information mapping TSN Streams to DetNet flows is needed only by the service proxy of MPLS edge nodes. The node needs TSN configuration for its TSN role, DetNet MPLS configuration for its DetNet role, and app-flow identification information, and this MUST be provisioned per DetNet flow.

Mapping between the DetNet and TSN management and control planes is out of scope, but the RFC highlights challenges. The management techniques are similar, while control plane protocols differ, for example RSVP-TE and MSRP behave differently. Because the DetNet network is one hop from the Ethernet perspective, some parameters such as delay may differ significantly, so its bandwidth is assumed to be set large enough for all the TSN flows it supports. Finding the egress for a stream with a multicast destination MAC address may be non-trivial.
sections.eli5: Someone has to set up the guest lists and decide which messages go in which envelope. How the two networks' managers talk to each other is left for later.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Security considerations for DetNet are covered in a separate Internet-Draft, and general ones are in RFC 8655. Considerations specific to the DetNet MPLS data plane are in RFC 8964. This document focuses on TSN Streams as the application flows, which the RFC says is already covered by those DetNet MPLS considerations. It adds no new security mechanisms of its own.
sections.eli5: The safety rules were already written elsewhere, and this RFC just points to them.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: This document has no IANA actions. Nothing needs to be registered for TSN to ride over DetNet MPLS as described here.
sections.eli5: No new numbers had to be added to any official list.
